summary: This standards-track memo defines the procedures for using the Kerberos V5 mechanism with the GSS-API. It updates RFC 1964 with incremental changes in response to developments since that document.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 4121 defines how Kerberos Version 5 works with the Generic Security Service API (GSS-API). It updates the message tokens so their encryption and checksum algorithms come from the negotiated key rather than identifiers in each token. The RFC updates RFC 1964 and has itself been updated by later RFCs.

subtitle: How Kerberos protects GSS-API messages with token formats tied to the negotiated key.

tldr.problem: The earlier Kerberos GSS-API mechanism put algorithm identifiers in per-message tokens, which does not fit the generic Kerberos cryptosystem framework.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 4121 derives purpose- and direction-specific keys from a session key or subkey, then defines MIC and Wrap tokens with sequence numbers and revised headers.
tldr.outcome: The new formats must be used with newer encryption types and may be used with older types when both peers support them. RFC 4121 updates RFC 1964 and is itself updated by RFC 5896, RFC 6112, RFC 6542, RFC 6649 and RFC 8062.

today: RFC 4121 is a Proposed Standard that updates RFC 1964. It has itself been updated by RFC 5896, RFC 6112, RFC 6542, RFC 6649 and RFC 8062.

sections.title: A Kerberos Mechanism for GSS-API
sections.content:
The Generic Security Service Application Program Interface (GSS-API) lets applications use security mechanisms through a common interface. RFC 1964 described the Kerberos Version 5 mechanism, including tokens for setting up a context and protecting messages. Its per-message tokens carried algorithm identifiers.

RFC 4121 uses the encryption and checksum algorithms associated with the session key or subkey established during context setup. It removes algorithm identifiers from the new per-message token layouts. These new formats MUST be used with newer encryption types; older types may use them when both peers know they support the formats.
sections.plainLanguage: GSS-API lets an application request security without defining Kerberos message details itself. This RFC updates how Kerberos protects messages by using the algorithms associated with the agreed session key.

sections.title: Deriving Keys for Each Message Purpose
sections.content:
RFC 4121 defines four key-usage values to derive keys for signing and sealing messages. The value depends on whether the sender is the context initiator or acceptor and whether the token is a MIC or Wrap token. Wrap key values are used even when the token does not provide confidentiality.

The base key is selected during context setup. An acceptor-asserted subkey takes precedence; otherwise an initiator-asserted subkey is used; if neither side asserts a subkey, the service-ticket session key is used. If an acceptor subkey is selected, later message tokens must indicate that fact. The GSS-API Quality of Protection value is ignored with these token formats.
sections.plainLanguage: Kerberos derives separate keys for each message direction and purpose from a session key or subkey. The peers follow the same order to choose that starting key.

sections.title: Establishing a Security Context
sections.content:
Context-establishment tokens use the generic GSS-API framing. Their inner token begins with a two-octet token identifier in big-endian order, followed by a Kerberos message: KRB_AP_REQ, KRB_AP_REP or KRB_ERROR. If the receiver sees an unknown identifier in the initial token, it returns GSS_S_CONTINUE_NEEDED and a KRB_ERROR with code KRB_AP_ERR_MSG_TYPE.

The authenticator checksum carries context flags, channel-binding information and optional delegation data. Its checksum type is 0x8003. The Bnd field contains an MD5 hash of the channel bindings, or 16 zero-valued octets when the caller supplies no bindings. Context-deletion tokens are empty; each peer deletes its local context independently.
sections.plainLanguage: Peers begin a security context by exchanging tokens that identify Kerberos request, reply or error messages. The setup checksum can carry requested services and information tying the context to a communication channel.

sections.title: MIC and Wrap Message Tokens
sections.content:
A MIC token protects data integrity and travels separately from the data. A Wrap token carries the data, either encrypted or in plaintext with a checksum. Neither new per-message token uses the generic framing used for context-establishment tokens.

Both formats include a token identifier, flags and an eight-octet sequence number. The sequence number is a 64-bit big-endian integer that increases after each token. A direction flag prevents a token sent in one direction from being accepted as a message in the reverse direction. A Wrap token also carries EC, which gives a filler or checksum length, and RRC, a count used to rotate token data. With confidentiality, the plaintext and a copy of the header are encrypted; without it, the checksum covers the data and header.
sections.plainLanguage: A MIC token lets the receiver check data without carrying the data itself. A Wrap token carries the data, with or without encryption. Both include a counter and direction information that are covered by the integrity check.

sections.title: Using the New Formats with Older Peers
sections.content:
Only new implementations recognize the token formats defined here. For encryption types that are not newer, implementations can use the sign or seal algorithms defined by RFC 1964. Retrying with the older format would require secure negotiation or an out-of-band choice, so the RFC recommends using the new format only when both peers are known to support it.

A receiver distinguishes token styles by examining the first octet. A value of 0x60 indicates generic GSS-API framing; otherwise the first two octets identify the token format. Identifiers from 0x60 0x00 through 0x60 0xFF are reserved, making this distinction unambiguous.
sections.plainLanguage: Older implementations do not understand these new tokens. Use them only when both peers are known to support them; otherwise the earlier RFC 1964 format is available for older encryption types.

sections.title: Channel Bindings and Cipher Selection
sections.content:
An acceptor may ignore channel bindings supplied by the initiator if the application does not provide bindings to GSS_Accept_sec_context and the acceptor does not prove that it has the same bindings. This can apply even when mutual authentication was requested. Applications that depend on channel bindings should account for this limitation.

The Key Distribution Center (KDC) chooses session-key types, and this mechanism does not negotiate algorithms with the acceptor. Administrators can restrict the types issued for a service, but doing so may also prevent other services using the same principal from receiving a stronger key type. The RFC says administrators should weigh that reduction in protection against interoperability.
sections.plainLanguage: An application should not assume the acceptor checked channel bindings unless the mechanism's conditions for checking them are met. The KDC chooses encryption types, so administrators balance compatibility with the protection provided by the available key types.
